description: Early blight is a common fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani. It affects tomato plants worldwide and can cause significant yield loss.
treatment: Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or azoxystrobin. Begin treatment when first symptoms appear and repeat every 7-10 days.
organic_treatment: Apply copper-based fungicides (Bordeaux mix) or neem oil spray every 7-14 days. Remove and destroy infected plant parts.
fertilizer: Apply balanced NPK fertilizer (10-10-10) with adequate potassium to strengthen plant immunity. Foliar spray with seaweed extract.
prevention_tips: Use disease-resistant varieties. Practice crop rotation (avoid planting tomatoes in same spot for 3+ years). Mulch to prevent soil splash. Water at base, not overhead. Ensure good air circulation.
symptoms: Dark brown to black spots with concentric rings (target-like pattern) on lower leaves. Leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely. Stem lesions may occur.

description: Late blight is a devastating disease caused by Phytophthora infestans. It spreads rapidly in cool, wet conditions and can destroy entire crops.
treatment: Apply systemic fungicides containing metalaxyl, mefenoxam, or cymoxanil. Start preventively during wet weather. Remove and destroy infected plants immediately.
organic_treatment: Apply copper hydroxide (Kocide) or Bacillus subtilis-based products. Ensure proper drainage. Remove infected plants to prevent spread.
fertilizer: Apply calcium-rich fertilizer to strengthen cell walls. Avoid excessive nitrogen which promotes lush growth susceptible to disease.
prevention_tips: Use resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation. Space plants for good air circulation. Monitor weather forecasts for favorable disease conditions. Remove volunteer solanaceous plants.
symptoms: Water-soaked lesions on leaves that turn brown and necrotic. White fuzzy growth on leaf undersides in humid conditions. Fruit develops firm, brown spots.

description: Leaf mold is caused by the fungus Passalora fulva (formerly Fulvia fulva). It thrives in high humidity and is common in greenhouse tomatoes.
treatment: Apply fungicides such as chlorothalonil or mancozeb. Improve greenhouse ventilation. Remove infected leaves promptly.
organic_treatment: Use neem oil or copper-based sprays. Increase air circulation. Prune lower leaves to reduce humidity around plants.
fertilizer: Maintain balanced nutrition with emphasis on potassium. Avoid excessive nitrogen.
prevention_tips: Ensure good ventilation in greenhouses. Avoid overcrowding. Use resistant varieties. Water at the base of plants.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow spots on upper leaf surface. Olive-green to brown velvety mold on lower leaf surface. Infected leaves may curl and drop.

description: Septoria leaf spot is caused by the fungus Septoria lycopersici. It is one of the most common and destructive tomato diseases.
treatment: Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil, copper, or mancozeb. Begin when first symptoms appear and continue throughout the season.
organic_treatment: Apply copper spray or neem oil. Remove all infected plant debris at end of season. Mulch to prevent soil splash.
fertilizer: Maintain adequate calcium levels. Use balanced fertilizer to keep plants vigorous.
prevention_tips: Remove and destroy infected leaves. Avoid working with plants when wet. Mulch heavily. Practice crop rotation. Use disease-free transplants.
symptoms: Small, circular spots with gray centers and dark margins on lower leaves. Spots may merge causing leaf death. Tiny black fruiting bodies visible in spots.

description: Bacterial spot is caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria. It causes significant damage to leaves and fruit.
treatment: Apply copper-based bactericides (copper hydroxide or copper oxychloride) combined with mancozeb. Start early in the season.
organic_treatment: Copper sprays are the primary organic option. Remove infected plant material. Avoid overhead watering.
fertilizer: Maintain plant vigor with balanced nutrition. Avoid high nitrogen which promotes succulent growth.
prevention_tips: Use bacterial spot-resistant varieties. Use disease-free seeds and transplants. Avoid working in fields when wet. Practice crop rotation.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked lesions on leaves that become brown and angular. Defoliation occurs with severe infection. Fruit spots are raised and scab-like.

description: The plant appears healthy with no visible signs of disease. Leaves are green and vigorous.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue regular care and monitoring.
organic_treatment: Maintain organic practices with compost tea and companion planting.
fertilizer: Apply balanced fertilizer as per growth stage. Side-dress with compost during fruiting.
prevention_tips: Continue good cultural practices: proper spacing, crop rotation, adequate watering, and regular inspection.
symptoms: No disease symptoms. Plant shows normal growth with green foliage and healthy fruit development.

description: Early blight caused by Alternaria solani affects potato foliage and can reduce tuber yield significantly.
treatment: Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or azoxystrobin. Begin at first sign of disease.
organic_treatment: Apply copper-based fungicides or neem oil. Remove and destroy infected foliage.
fertilizer: Apply adequate potassium to strengthen plants. Maintain soil pH around 5.5-6.5.
prevention_tips: Use certified seed potatoes. Practice 3-year crop rotation. Hill soil around plants to cover tubers. Avoid overhead irrigation.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings on lower leaves. Yellowing and death of infected tissue. Stem lesions at soil line.

description: Late blight caused by Phytophthora infestans is the same disease that caused the Irish potato famine. It can destroy entire fields rapidly.
treatment: Apply systemic fungicides with metalaxyl or mefenoxam. Remove and destroy infected plants immediately to prevent spread.
organic_treatment: Apply copper hydroxide sprays. Destroy infected plants. Ensure good field drainage.
fertilizer: Avoid excessive nitrogen. Maintain adequate phosphorus for root development.
prevention_tips: Use resistant varieties. Plant in well-drained soil. Monitor weather for favorable conditions. Destroy volunteer potatoes and solanaceous weeds.
symptoms: Water-soaked lesions on leaves turning brown. White mold growth on leaf undersides in humid weather. Tuber rot with reddish-brown discoloration.

description: The potato plant is healthy with vigorous growth and no visible disease symptoms.
organic_treatment: Continue with organic soil management and compost applications.
fertilizer: Apply balanced fertilizer with emphasis on potassium for tuber development.
prevention_tips: Monitor regularly for early disease detection. Maintain proper hilling and irrigation practices.
symptoms: No disease symptoms. Plants show normal growth with healthy green foliage.

description: Brown spot is caused by the fungus Bipolaris oryzae. It affects rice foliage, glumes, and grains.
treatment: Apply fungicides containing iprodione, propiconazole, or tricyclazole. Seed treatment with carbendazim before planting.
organic_treatment: Apply Pseudomonas fluorescens-based biofungicide. Use neem cake or neem oil spray. Ensure proper field sanitation.
fertilizer: Apply adequate silicon to strengthen plant tissues. Balanced NPK with proper micronutrients.
prevention_tips: Use healthy, disease-free seeds. Practice proper spacing. Ensure good field drainage. Avoid excessive nitrogen.
symptoms: Oval to circular brown spots on leaves with yellow halo. Spots on grain (glumes) reducing quality. Severe infection causes leaf drying.

description: Leaf blast is caused by Magnaporthe oryzae. It is one of the most destructive rice diseases worldwide.
treatment: Apply fungicides containing tricyclazole, isoprothiolane, or azoxystrobin. Seed treatment with carbendazim or tricyclazole.
organic_treatment: Apply Pseudomonas fluorescens. Use resistant varieties. Balance nitrogen fertilizer application.
fertilizer: Avoid excessive nitrogen. Apply potash to strengthen plant resistance. Use silica-based fertilizers.
prevention_tips: Use blast-resistant varieties. Avoid dense planting. Apply split nitrogen doses. Use proper water management.
symptoms: Diamond-shaped lesions with gray centers and dark brown margins on leaves. Lesions may girdle leaves causing death. In severe cases, entire leaves dry up.

description: The rice plant is healthy with no signs of disease.
organic_treatment: Continue with organic amendments and biological pest management.
fertilizer: Apply balanced fertilizer as per growth stage recommendations.
prevention_tips: Maintain proper water levels and field sanitation.
symptoms: No disease symptoms. Plants show normal growth with green foliage and healthy tillers.

description: Northern leaf blight is caused by the fungus Exserohilum turcicum. It is one of the most common and destructive corn diseases.
treatment: Apply fungicides containing propiconazole, tebuconazole, or azoxystrobin. Begin at tasseling or silking stage.
organic_treatment: Use resistant hybrids. Remove and destroy infected residue. Apply biological control agents like Bacillus subtilis.
fertilizer: Maintain adequate nitrogen and potassium. Avoid excessive nitrogen that favors disease development.
prevention_tips: Plant resistant hybrids. Practice crop rotation with non-host crops. Bury crop residue. Avoid overhead irrigation.
symptoms: Long, cigar-shaped grayish-tan lesions on leaves. Lesions can be 1-6 inches long. Under humid conditions, dark fungal growth appears on lesions.

description: Common rust is caused by the fungus Puccinia sorghi. It appears as rust-colored pustules on leaves.
treatment: Apply fungicides with triazole or strobilurin chemistry when rust pustules first appear. Most modern hybrids have good resistance.
organic_treatment: Plant resistant varieties. Remove alternate host plants (certain grasses). Apply neem-based products.
fertilizer: Maintain balanced nutrition with adequate potassium for disease resistance.
prevention_tips: Use resistant hybrids. Scout fields early. Most hybrids have adequate resistance, so chemical control is rarely needed.
symptoms: Small, round to elongated rust-colored pustules on both leaf surfaces. Pustules contain powdery orange spores. Severe infection causes leaf yellowing and death.

description: The maize/corn plant is healthy with no visible disease symptoms.
fertilizer: Apply balanced NPK fertilizer as per growth stage.
prevention_tips: Continue good agricultural practices including proper spacing and irrigation.
symptoms: No disease symptoms. Plants show normal growth with healthy green leaves and well-developed ears.

description: Bacterial blight (also called angular leaf spot) is caused by Xanthomonas citri pv. malvacearum. It affects all above-ground parts of cotton plants.
treatment: Apply copper-based bactericides. Use seed treatment with antibiotics or hot water treatment before planting. Remove infected plants.
organic_treatment: Apply copper hydroxide sprays. Use certified disease-free seed. Practice strict field sanitation.
fertilizer: Apply balanced fertilizer. Avoid excessive nitrogen which favors disease development.
prevention_tips: Use resistant varieties. Use certified disease-free seed. Practice crop rotation. Avoid working in fields when wet.
symptoms: Angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn dark brown to black. Spots have a greasy appearance. Stem and boll lesions also occur. Boll infection causes staining of lint.

description: The cotton plant is healthy with no visible disease symptoms.
organic_treatment: Continue with organic amendments and biological pest management.
fertilizer: Apply balanced NPK with adequate potassium for boll development.
prevention_tips: Maintain proper plant spacing and field sanitation.
symptoms: No disease symptoms. Plants show normal growth with healthy foliage and bolls.
